summary: Defines a DNS resource record type that maps domain names to NSAP addresses, the address format used by OSI networks. It works with any NSAP address format. It is historic.

eli5.summary: It teaches the internet's name book how to store an old kind of network address next to a name.

questions: map domain name to nsap address
how to map domain name to nsap
subtitle: How the DNS was taught to store OSI network addresses (NSAPs) under a domain name, and to look them up in reverse.

tldr.problem: Operators running OSI's CLNP in the Internet had to debug with numeric NSAP addresses and a shared name/address file, which lacked a central coordinator and scaled poorly.
tldr.mechanism: A new DNS resource record, NSAP (TYPE 22), maps a domain name to a binary NSAP. Reverse lookups reuse the PTR record under the NSAP.INT domain, with the NSAP's hex digits reversed one per label.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is now marked Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1348 and RFC 1637, and the unit metadata lists RFC 9121 as updating it.

today: RFC 1706 is marked Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1348 and RFC 1637, and it is listed as updated by RFC 9121.

sections.title: Why NSAPs Needed Names
sections.content:
OSI lower layer protocols, including the connectionless network protocol (CLNP) and its routing protocols, were deployed in some parts of the Internet. Maintaining and debugging CLNP is easier if the Domain Name System can map between names and NSAP (network service access point) addresses.

At the time, debugging with CLNP ping and traceroute got harder as deployment grew, because only numeric NSAPs were available. People kept and swapped a configuration file of name/NSAP pairs, similar to hosts.txt. The RFC names two problems: nobody coordinated the file, and a hosts.txt-style approach scales badly.

The memo defines one new resource record for name-to-NSAP mapping. It works with any NSAP format. It treats DNS only as a way to publish addresses; registration of NSAPs stays with the authority described in ISO 8348.
sections.eli5: Long number addresses are hard to remember, so people kept a messy shared list of names. This gives them a proper name book instead.

sections.title: How NSAPs Are Structured
sections.content:
NSAPs are hierarchical so that authority can be handed down and routing stays efficient. The RFC asks DNS resolvers and servers to know little or nothing in advance about NSAP structure, because delegated authorities define their own fields. It describes NSAPs as a tree whose root is ISO 8348 and whose first level is the one-octet Authority and Format Identifiers (AFIs).

As an example it walks through the U.S. GOSIP layout: AFI 47, then the value 0005 that NIST obtained, then a format identifier 80, then a three-octet field allocated to network operators through GSA, and so on down to the last octet.

That last octet is the NSelector (NSel), which identifies the CLNP user. Because one system may have several, all NSAPs stored in the DNS use NSel=0, and the application decides which value to use. When CLNP carries TCP and UDP, the NSel is the IANA-registered IP PROTO value.

For readability NSAPs are written with periods between hex groups, such as 47.0005.80.005a00. The periods never appear in DNS packets.
sections.eli5: An NSAP is like a long address with country, city, street and house number. The last number says which person in the house should get the message, and the name book always writes zero there.

sections.title: The NSAP Resource Record
sections.content:
The record has the mnemonic NSAP and TYPE code 22 (decimal). A query asks the resolver for an NSAP record for a domain name, much like an IP address lookup. The record follows the standard resource record layout of RFC 1035, with these fields:

  • NAME: the owner name.
  • TYPE: 22. CLASS: IN, code 1.
  • TTL: a 32-bit signed integer giving seconds the record may be cached; zero means use only for the transaction in progress.
  • RDLENGTH: an unsigned 16-bit length in octets.
  • RDATA: the binary NSAP exactly as it would appear in a CLNP source or destination address field.

The RFC's sample NSAP, 39840f80005a0000000001e13708002010726e00, has an RDLENGTH of 20. NSAP records cause no additional section processing.
sections.eli5: The record is a small card with the name on the front and the long number address on the back, plus a note saying how long to keep the card before checking again.

sections.title: Finding a Name from an NSAP
sections.content:
Going the other way uses the existing PTR record from RFC 1035. That record normally lives under IN-ADDR.ARPA for IPv4 addresses. For NSAPs it lives under the NSAP.INT domain.

To build the name, take the NSAP's hex digits (nibbles), reverse their order, treat each nibble as its own subdomain label, and append NSAP.INT. A resolver then asks for a PTR record at that name. The RFC suggests that user interfaces let people type NSAPs in their natural order and ignore stray periods.
sections.eli5: To look up a name from a number, you spell the number backwards, one digit at a time, and look in a special section of the book.

sections.title: Master Files and Security
sections.content:
In master files, NSAP and PTR records follow Section 5 of RFC 1035. The NSAP record adds one new RDATA format: 0x followed by a variable-length string of hex digits. It is case-insensitive, and periods after the 0x may be added for readability but are not sent in queries or zone transfers.

The RFC includes a sample zone for nsap.nist.gov with hosts such as bsdi1 and routers such as cisco1, each with an NSAP record and often A records, plus a matching reverse zone with PTR records.

The security section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.eli5: The examples show a real-looking page from the name book, with computers and their long numbers. The RFC does not talk about safety at all.
